The release of information regarding the use of the reserve during a particular month takes place on the second day of the following month. Information relating to the month of January will be published tomorrow.

I explained yesterday that one of the reasons we have to borrow in foreign markets is that there is a lot of liquidity in Canada. The provinces are not borrowing abroad, and we have decided to substitute for them in that respect. That is why we are borrowing abroad. We want to maintain the flow of capital which is needed because we have a balance of payments deficit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers. Just an hour from now the minister will be announcing at a press conference outside of parliamentary scrutiny a multimillion dollar handout for the pulp and paper industry in Canada, which I think is totally irresponsible, instead of bringing the matter before parliament. Considering that the big six in the pulp and paper industry which control most of the industry have made profits in 1977 of $160 million and have just announced a 150 per cent increase in those profits for 1978 up to $379 million, can he tell the House why the government is giving away to this industry many millions of dollars at this time for the development of resources instead of insisting that when they are making profits in the

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: PULP AND PAPER-RETENTION OF PERCENTAGE OF PROFITS FOR INVESTMENT IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite correct that the forest products industry in this last year or so has enjoyed a good cash flow and good profits. It is very much related to the temporary situation with regard to the Canadian dollar, a competitive advantage they enjoy now but one which I do not think anyone anticipates may last very long, and one on which they cannot count.
In the meantime, I think everyone who examines this very important industry in terms of the number of jobs it provides in this country, the volume of its export trade in the amount of $8 billion a year, and who examines the significance of this, would realize it is in the Canadian interest to ensure there is investment and modernization of plants, because it is facing severe competition in the longer term from the United States and from other parts of the world. It needs modernization and it needs forest management. All those aspects were recommended by the task force on the forest products industry in which both labour and management joined. We are responding to that and insisting, of course, that any contribution or grant from the government is matched at least three to one by the companies themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have given you notice of my question of privilege, although following the last several days of question period I am tempted
Privilege-Mr. Wenman
to raise another one. I have given notice of my intention to raise the question regarding the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts).
Section 23 of the Canada Council Act specifically states that the chairman of the council must submit an annual report to the Secretary of State and, I quote, "provision shall be made for a review thereof (of the annual report) by parliament". To date there has been no review of the Canada Council's annual report or of the council's mandate. Of course, when the estimates of the Secretary of State's department are before the appropriate standing committee, the Canada Council and its staff respond to various questions put forth. The Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts has, however, never had the council's annual report referred to it, nor has there been a review by parliament as legislated by the House of Commons.
There are several pieces of legislation which place similar demands upon the government as found in clause 23 of the Canada Council Act.
Section 46 of the Anti-Inflation Board Act obliged the government, if it wished to extend the controls period beyond their December 31 expiry date, to present a motion on the order in council which would outline the extension. Clearly if the order in council was given to extend the controls, then three days hence a motion would have been laid before parliament.
Section 20 of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act states:
The House of Commons shall, within the first fifteen days next after the expiration of that period that the House of Commons is sitting, take up the motion and consider the matter of the objective.
Clearly, if the procedure in section 20 of this legislation is followed through, the House of Commons must debate that motion.
Finally, section 18(2) of the Government Organization Act obligates a member of the Queen's Privy Council to propose a motion in the House when the governor in council creates a new ministry of state by order in council.
If the government chose not to fulfil the obligations in the above pieces of legislation it would be an indisputable breach of privilege. I, along with other members, would not be able to discharge my duties in this House.
On June 27 in the House of Commons I brought to the attention of the Secretary of State the provision for the review within the legislation and asked him if he would refer the annual report to a parliamentary committee. The Secretary of State replied:
I would have absolutely no objection to such a course of action, if the members of the committee express their desire to meet through the chairman, and that such should take place.
Immediately I sent a memo to all members of parliament asking them if they felt there should be a review of the Canada Council. I asked for these memos to be returned to my office. Members from all sides of the House were in support that the legislation should be followed and that a review should take

February 1, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Wenman
place. I forwarded copies of the memos to the Secretary of State and asked him to sponsor in the House the necessary order of reference to the committee so that I might discharge my duty. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to comment on the allegations made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman). It seems to me that the hon. member has confused two questions, and as a result it has lead to erroneous conclusions. The first is the question of the obligations imposed on the Secretary of State by section 23 of the Canada Council Act. The motion of the hon. gentleman refers to the refusal of the Secretary of State to fulfil the obligation conferred by section 23. If members of the House were kind enough to read section 23 of the Canada Council Act they would see that the obligation referred to in section 23 is an obligation which attaches to the chairman of the council, not to the Secretary of State.
I would be pleased to transfer to the House a report of the Canada Council. Indeed I do transfer to the House reports of the various agencies which report to parliament through me as soon as I receive them. However, I cannot perform the deliverance of that which I do not have, and I do not have the report of the Canada Council. If there is a failure of obligation under section 23 of the Canada Council Act, it lies not on the part of the Secretary of State but on the part of the Canada Council which is not yet finished that report.
The second matter, which is a distinct and different matter, to which the hon. member has referred, is the question of whether the House or, more specifically, the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts should conduct an inquiry into the operations of the Canada Council. I have said in the past that it is not for me to direct the members of the committee as to how they should work. The proper course of action for a member who wishes to see a certain matter discussed by a committee is to address that question to the steering committee so that the steering committee may consider the matter and make whatever recommendation it desires.
Whether the hon. member accumulates a petition, with goodness knows how many names of members of the House who are concerned to have that happen, is not strictly speaking relevant in that manner. What is relevant is that the steering committee make a recommendation. If that is the concern the member has, that such an inquiry should be undertaken, he should not take his concern to me but to the steering committee and ask that committee, via the chairman, to make a recommendation to me.
If he were to say to me, do I think this is a good moment to undertake such a review, I would say to the hon. member, as I have said to him, frankly, no. The reason why it is not at this time especially appropriate to undertake such a review is that we have under way, as the hon. member knows, in the Department of Secretary of State, a review of the government's cultural policy, our strategy of funding to the arts. It would seem to be much more valuable to the members of the committee to look at the Canada Council and its operations in that larger context which I hope will be available soon, and
February 1, 1979

available to members of the committee soon. A useful discussion of the Canada Council in isolation from that wider perspective should not be undertaken at this point.
The hon. member, as a member of that committee, and in fact all members of the committee, do now and have always had the opportunity to cross-examine the Canada Council on its operations when the estimates in the normal way are before the committee. That right, duty, and obligation have not been taken away from the committee. They are still there. The possibility of the hon. member throwing himself fully into that work, as he has done in the past, is still there. There is no lack of opportunity to examine the Canada Council and its operations in the normal process.
If the hon. member is asking whether we should have a special inquiry, I say that is not the best thing to undertake at this time given the fact there is a more general review under way which will be a more suitable framework for discussing this question, and the question of artistic policy generally.
To sum up what I have said, if his complaint is that I have not ordered, asked for, or agreed to an insurance of instruction to the committee, to undertake an examination of the Canada Council, I would say that is so. It is not primarily my responsibility to take that position. I do not think it would be a wise action to take at this time for the reasons I have just discussed. That may be a matter of debate between the hon. member and myself. However, if his question is whether I have somehow slighted him and the House in general by a failure to meet the obligation of section 23, I must point out that the obligations of section 23 of the act refer not to me but to the members of the Canada Council.

Order, please. The hon. member will know that in raising this matter pursuant to Standing Order 26, of which he has given me notice as he has said, he is raising again for the Chair a very difficult problem because the provisions of Standing Order 26 require some initial decision on the part of the Chair as to whether the matter is in fact, as described in the language of paragraph 16(a) of the Standing Order, a genuine emergency.
I want to refer to some language I have used previously. On January 24, 1977, a matter was raised with respect to unemployment levels. On December 6, 1977, the matter of unemployment conditions was again raised in an application pursuant to this rule. While I will not bore the House with the details of my language at those times, it related to the fact that this was a chronic problem in the country regarding an aspect of the economy, and as a chronic problem it ought not to be considered as the kind of emergency which is the proper subject of applications pursuant to Standing Order 26.
I said the same thing with respect to the value of the dollar, which surely falls under the same general condition.
However, I am sure the hon. member will know that on February 22 of last year, pursuant to a joint application by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), I reviewed all the provisions of this standing order and this same application with respect to the level of the dollar at that time. I then concluded that all other conditions with respect to this standing order had been fulfilled, and having some doubt as to whether this matter at that time constituted the kind of emergency envisaged by the standing order I extended the benefit of that doubt to the hon. members and granted a debate.
I now must consider the matter again as a result of the application by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). I did so in February of last year and departed for that one time from this line of reasoning. I think I have highlighted the difficulty the Chair is placed under with respect to chronic problems in the country when they are made the subject matter of applications pursuant to this standing order. The Chair is obviously put into the invidious position of saying, for example, "If 7 per cent unemployment is a chronic problem, does 8 per cent become an emergency?" The level of the dollar has been at 83 cents, 84 cents or 85 cents. Does a further one cent drop constitute a continuing chronic economic problem in the country, or does it at a certain level become a crisis or an emergency which should be the subject matter of an application pursuant to this standing order? I think the hon. member and other hon. members will understand that this is not the

The House resumed from Wednesday, January 31, 1979, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde (for Mr. Reid) that Bill C-9, respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to resume from yesterday my comments in connection with Bill C-9 which is, in my opinion, one of the most negative ever introduced in the House of Commons. It has been motivated by fear. The government is fearful and, not unlike the events in October 1970, it would like to stir up another crisis but in a different way. With Bill C-9, the confrontation is restricted to Canada, our country.
There are some points in that bill which I would like to raise. It gives a discretionary and discriminatory authority to the government to choose the provinces where in theory a referendum could be held. This means that the bill would not necessarily have a national scope or fall under a truly federal jurisdiction. If it were passed, it would be possible to decide as early as tomorrow to hold a referendum in four Canadian provinces and then on the basis of the results obtained try to enforce a particular decision on that province. This is certainly one of the dangers of this bill. Moreover, the government comes up with a rather doubtful argument to the effect that when the referendum takes place in Quebec, the Parti Quebe-cois could bias the question and phrase it in such a way that people might not exactly understand its meaning. As far as this is concerned, let me refer to the question which was asked during the 1942 plebiscite held by a Liberal government. The question was not particularly clear and I suggest there is no guarantee that the question asked on a federal referendum would be any clearer. In 1942 the question was as follows: Would you agree to discharge the government from any obligation resulting from previous commitments restricting the mobilization procedures for military service? No reference

whatsoever was made to conscription. Yet, we all know that this plebiscite was held with a view to drafting Canadians into the armed forces, but it was put in milder terms to entice people into supporting conscription in Canada. We all know what the outcome was. The province of Quebec alone voted against conscription, all the others were in favour. Maybe the English version was clearer. Who knows! That is one of the dangers. We cannot assume that the federal government will necessarily be more honest than the Parti Quebecois in Quebec in the way the question will be put. There is a danger of distorting the question. We are assuming that that is what Quebec will do. But Quebec can also assume that we, the federal government, will do the same. We are knee-deep in assumptions.
Also, this legislation is restrictive to an extent. It authorizes referenda only on constitutional matters. Why not other issues such as capital punishment, social policy? We could even go one better, like some countries and some American states, into tax fields, taxation, the people could be consulted on those issues as well. Also, this bill does not allow a citizen to ask for a referendum.
A province is not allowed to pressure the federal level to a referendum. Neither is a group of citizens. Only the governor in council may request a referendum at the federal level. This limits the will of the citizens. I think that such a possibility in Bill C-9 might be more palatable than the restrictive measures which exist now. I suggest the government should consider changing its bill to include at least part of what the opposition is seeking. I feel the federal government exists to maintain harmony in the interest of all Canadians and that it should take into account any constructive suggestion made by the opposition. And I hope that when we reach the committee stage, it will introduce amendments or at least propose some changes to this bill.
There is another clause in the bill which limits the broadcasting time allocated to the federal government and federal and provincial parties to three and one-quarter hours. I must admit that at first sight it does not seem too fair to me. There is a fairly large number of provincial parties across Canada and the air time allotted to those parties will be very restricted. This legislation goes even further when it provides that a party with one member sitting in a provincial legislature will be recognized as a political party. This is not recognized at the federal level but only at the provincial level. They want to divide and rule. There is a danger in monopolizing air time: the federal government could then make a national issue out of it. But if a province or a provincial political party is against the option, it would be restricted within a small region to express its views. This is not giving equal opportunities to all.
One thing that is often forgotten is that if we have a federal parliament, a federal government, it is because there are provinces, and if all the provinces decided overnight to become
February 1, 1979

a specific entity, a separate country, there would be no more federal government. If the federal government were to disappear, the provinces would remain. I think the essence of the Canadian confederation was precisely to acknowledge particular entities, provinces with specific areas of jurisdiction which decided to pool some sectors of activity saying: we will create a central government with powers to administer jurisdictions of our own choosing.
In 1968, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected because he promised to solve national unity problems. Well, if national unity problems have been solved, I wonder in what sector it happened. Things are worsening on the constitutional side because of the adamant attitude of the Liberal government. It does not seem that our Prime Minister wants to reverse this situation. He is chiefly responsible for the state of crisis we are experiencing now and now he will go before the Canadian people pretending to be the saviour of the nation. Some saviour!
In the ten years he has been in power he has tried everything to reduce the jurisdiction of the provinces, to centralize at the federal level, and this loss of powers has gradually led us to the present crisis which we are now trying to solve by means of national confrontation within Canada.
I suggest we should seriously, in our conscience, think that the Fathers of Confederation did not want a divided country, they tried to build a united country by establishing a fair and equitable division of powers. We are no longer talking about a Canadian confederation, the word is federation. Not the same thing by a long shot. A federation is a group of states accountable to a central government, while a confederation is made up of sovereign nations which decide to pool certain sectors of activity, in their common interest. I believe we should come back to a real confederation to establish harmony and national unity in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have already heard many different comments on the bill respecting public referendums in Canada. First, let us look at the reasons for this decision by the government. We could dwell on some problems which most hon. members know and which are the reasons for the decisions the government made concerning this new piece of legislation. This formula of consultation has already been used in different countries. There are probably a few advantages to it, provided the many disadvantages which could arise in the style used in the drafting of the questions which will be asked are foreseen in the implementation of the rules.
The general organization of a referendum can be compared with the organization of a general election each time the elements are similar. For example, in both cases there is a national vote and the electors are the same, namely those who are on the permanent election list. The same officers will probably be used and they will probably have the same responsibilities. Finally, the details on the material organization will
Referenda
have to be established in consideration of the experience acquired; it is a matter of convenience and of efficiency.
What gives value and usefulness to a referendum, advisory though it may be, is the attitude of the government of the day in relation with the issue of the referendum, namely whether or not it is prepared to give consideration to the will of the public and consider itself bound by such will. A government can always promise that it will accept the result of a referendum. That is what Mr. Wilson's British government did before the referendum on maintaining British participation in the European Common Market. In our parliamentary system, where the written constitution makes no reference to referenda, it is necessary to enact legislation concerning the holding of a referendum and the way it will be organized. That can be useful in certain circumstances. Everything depends on the events which occur and on the way in which it is used. That is what was done in countries where the parliamentary tradition is similar to ours, namely in Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand. In all those instances a bill was introduced respecting a referendum on a specific matter and even spelling out the question to be put to the voters. In the newspaper Le Devoir of December 17, 1976 there was an article entitled: "Spain Referendum Lesson" summarized somewhat the inconveniences and advantages that can result from a referendum. After having pointed out that, of those who voted, 94.2 per cent voted yes and 2.6 per cent of the population had abstained from voting, it said, and I quote:
This is where some truths must be grasped and the real question put. Might the watchword to abstain not be a strategic error, all the more unforgiveable that it fed-the success of the referendum has proved it clearly-on a false perception of Spanish realities? Ideologically speaking, some will claim great democratic ideals while rejecting compromise. That position could very well be justifiable. But does one defend democracy better when proving one's weaknesses?
I point out, however, that in these times of economic problems of all sorts it may not be as advantageous as some believe to make a permanent institution of a formula that has not been tried.
If we spent more time discovering the reasons which have led to our discussing this bill, we might discover that the most ingenious means would be to solve, beforehand the problems that are likely to crop up later. I remember full well that referendums have been asked for on various occasions in Canada, all bearing on very important topics. I shall mention the suggestion made to the government that a referendum be held before the bill on capital punishment was passed. For reasons that are difficult to explain, our administrators did not deem it wise to agree to those suggestions, but the fact remains they would have given solid reasons to the legislators and so enabled them to give a better orientation to legislation in that field.
In the last few years, we have noticed that polls of all sorts have become quite fashionable. Public opinion poll firms are developing very sophisticated questionnaires to submit to their
2800

February 1, 1979
Referenda
patients. However they are far from being ready to point out under the group "undecided" the increasing number of those who should be more properly included under the group "disgusted". I also remember reading somewhere what seem to me to be useful advice concerning referendums, namely that a policy of over-control could jeopardize the equal opportunities provided to the options involved.
In a report published in the newspaper Le Devoir on October 21, 1977, entitled "The Referendum War" by Robert Decary, the following could be read:
The campaign for the provincial referendum has hardly been launched in Quebec and already Ottawa has decided to organize its own referendum. It is fair play. Even if the contents of the bill have not yet been disclosed, it is possible that in the near future Quebeckers will be called to vote twice about belonging to the Canadian nation. No provision for the withdrawal of a province appears in the British North America Act, so it seems that Ottawa as much as Quebec could hold its own vote.
It is a clear indication of a sick political system when two levels of government can in turn and each in its own way legislate in the same field; and this is no doubt a further reason to treat the "patient" and to make sure that under the new system, such a situation cannot be repeated. But for the moment, we will have to live with the system and submit to the rules of the game.
In 1942, we had some kind of public consultation in the form of a plebiscite. Many certainly remember the reactions to the announcement of that plebiscite.
The "yes" won nationally by 63.7 per cent to 36.3 per cent. So the country as a whole agreed to release the government from earlier promises. The kind of crisis that followed stirred many Canadians and changed several ideas. It is often when two nations are fiercely opposed that one can measure their vitality. I mentioned that kind of consultation, which was not a referendum strictly speaking, in order to show that one must be careful when holding a public consultation in a country like ours. Since the events that took place in Canada in 1976, all citizens and their governments were led no doubt to reconsider carefully their convictions and their position.
In an article published in Selections du Reader's Digest for the month of May, 1977, and entitled "Confederation in Danger" I read the following by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who sits in this House, which I think is quite relevant and I quote:
We must choose between the blind pursuit of our individual interests and the common good. We must give up the narrow-minded visions we have of Canada at times and consider everyone's needs and desires.
And he went on:
The direction taken by political leaders will be of prime importance because it will provide leadership; yet, they can do nothing without the support of every Canadian. The federal government will have to consider the consequences of its actions in the various areas of the country; Canadians for their part will have to try to ponder the effects of their statements, their actions and their individual reactions.
The article ends on this:
Maintaining Canadian unity always had a price. We must be prepared to compromise, to make concessions, even reluctantly. The fate of our country depends above all on our moderation and our will to survive. We are now going through a difficult test and we will know shortly if we are worthy of our heritage.
I have already stated in this House that our duty as legislators would be to allow all Canadians to live as heirs instead of
being perpetually indebted. If the government would really try to find an effective remedy to cure that sickness called fear of the future instead of legislating on referendum issues, we would avoid many difficulties, most of which result from our ineffective financial system. When we consider the damage caused by this system which produces indebted heirs, we find many causes which should be understood so that we can put some order in the present confusion.
However, I recognize that in the history of some countries many referendums have been held, sometimes on constitutional issues or to find a solution to controversial matters. Between 1911 and 1928, six referendums were held in New Zealand on prohibition and the sale of alcoholic beverages. Since then they have used that kind of popular vote many times.
In the United States, they held referendums at the very beginning of that nation. At the declaration of independence in 1776, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Rhode Island had their constitution approved by a direct vote. In 1778, Massachusetts was the first state to have recourse to that practice for its constitution which was rejected in public meetings across the land. Some authors maintain that it was the first time legislation was subject to a popular vote by way of a referendum.
On November 12, 1933, Adolf Hitler held a plebiscite at the same time as a general election. This election was held to obtain approval for a unique list of candidates to the Reichstag and the referendum to get approval for the withdrawal of Germany from the League of Nations. As a matter of fact, Hitler often used a referendum to gain support for his foreign policy. After his rise to power, he used the referendum essentially to show the other countries that his teams had the general support of the population.
We could ask ourselves this question: Of what use would future referendums be? Of course, they would be used to answer or to try to answer questions or problems about which the government must make decisions, but which could cause electoral embarrassment among a large sector of the population. We must recognize that a government must often take certain action which goes against the interests of certain groups. The concept of referendum could therefore be used to justify unpopular policies. Thus, in certain conditions, a referendum could become a strategy much more than a democratization of power. There are many problems too complex for a referendum to solve.
Let us consider for instance our energy problems; they are so complex that the experts themselves do not agree. Should we use a referendum to determine whether or not to develop nuclear energy? The citizens would not know what to decide because they are all more or less afraid of radiation. It would be difficult to use the results of a referendum to develop a long term energy policy. Just as if doctors asked their patients to choose their own therapy and medication.
In summary, referendums are political strategies much more than they are an effective means of popular participation in

February 1, 1979

the affairs of the state. Even if white papers are published on the subject, this does not necessarily mean that the intentions of the government are as pure as driven snow. We sometimes hear about separation and even subdivision. We must not forget that there are citizens with separatist ideas throughout the country. Fortunately, there are not that many of them at the present time. Flowever, at the proper time, it would be wiser to keep the debate on a conversational level, which could eventually lead to a Canadian union based on new and realistic concepts.
It is too late to rewrite the history of our country but we could find a formula of agreement in our modern Canada which would allow us to carry on together, to work in harmony and to develop our enormous potential of resources. Perhaps we could try to develop a few minds which appear to me far too proud to recognize the rights of others at the appropriate time. It is not because we lack legislation in our country, we might even have too much of it. The referendum bill might just be one more law out of many which, most of the time, are written in such a way that they cannot be understood.
Lately I had the opportunity to read in Le Devoir of March 29, 1977 an article about the new government in France and I want to quote an extract of a speech which was given by the French president on that occasion where he attributed to the new government the two following tasks, and I quote:
-First of all, our economy being on the way to recovery, we must pursue in that direction as it is vital for France and for the French. Your standard of living and your jobs depend on that recovery.
Then we must launch a 12-month action program accompanied by specific objectives. This program will have to meet the concrete areas of concern of the French and contain simple measures, explained in plain words easily understandable by everyone."
That is what we forget to do here when we write our bills. They are always very complicated. I remember drawing the attention of the members of the House to the fact that our laws are written in style which is far too complicated. We would need to seek formulas easily understood by everyone.
On April 4, 1978, Le Droit of Ottawa reported the first part of a speech made by Mr. Gerald Beaudoin, a member of the Pepin-Robarts Task Force on Canadian Unity. He was invited to comment on the constitutionality of the referendum. I quote a part of his speech on constitutional jurisdiction:
In 1969, under the Bertrand government, the Quebec legislature studied an organic bill on a consultative referendum. The Levesque government tabled its referendum bill in 1977. The constitution definitely grants a legislative assembly as well as the central government the authority to pass legislation respecting referenda on issues which come under their respective jurisdictions.
In the last few years much has been said about the constitution of Canada, now to amend, now to repatriate and more recently to renew it, emphasizing what it should be and seldom what it was, stressing the distribution of powers and educational and linguistic guarantees without realizing that we were reducing the 147 initial clauses of this act down to 4 or 5.
The constitution is more than a cluster of powers or rights which may be amended, repatriated or reformulated. It also means a political way of life, a choice of institutions, an almost
Referenda
invisible structure within which every citizen exercises his rights and without which he might have no right at all or exercise them differently. The constitution is the basis and the guarantee of social order.
We should take a more comprehensive and concrete approach to this and provide a more specific framework for the discussions which have been at a standstill for far too long. Our institutions have been set up only to serve the people that founded them and when they have become obsolete it is time to amend or replace them so that they get closer to their objective.
After 110 years of Confederation, Canada is facing the vital need and the moral obligation created by the parties concerned to reassess its attitude and position in a modern world. Our task now is to build the kind of Canada we would like to live in, not one which is imposed upon us from the outside, this does not imply a rejection of our past, but rather a positive, forward-looking attitude and a progressive, humanistic outlook.
Our past is gone by. The present quickly ebbs into the past. We must build the future, not only our own but that of our country and our fellow citizens because only in the future shall we be able to find gratification for our present yearnings and desires. History has decided that Anglophones and Francophones should share the same country as partners, albeit unequal, who have survived in the midst of many difficulties. All Canadians, within and without Quebec, can overcome their fears, prejudices, frustrations and resentment and learn to live together in a true spirit of brotherhood. In our country two races, two glorious histories are living side by side with just one common future. Every Canadian has the duty to make sure that our hopes will be fulfilled.

al ones that are important in people's minds, for example, the question of capital punishment and that of abortion. Those types of questions could come to a more satisfactory resolution if they were dealt with by referendum. However, the government does not seem disposed to consult Canadians on matters of that kind. I believe it is clear to every member of this House that a vast majority of the population, approximately 70 per cent to 80 per cent, would like to see capital punishment in effect in Canada. But because of the operation of our present system that will is frustrated and thwarted. As a result, people have come to believe they have no representation in this chamber.
In one respect I am pleased that the government is not saying absolutely that the general citizenry is forbidden from expressing a direct opinion, but I feel a means could be provided in this legislation by which citizens at large could determine what type of question they would like to see dealt with by referenda on an initiative basis.
The present legislation allows the government the absolute right and discretion concerning what questions will be asked. It has been pointed out before that a referendum has never been lost in Canada. We do not have a long history on the use of referenda. Some people have said what history we do have is not particularly happy when one considers the results of the two referenda that were used in the first and second world wars with respect to conscription. Many people believe that some of the problems that exist in the country today flow directly from the use of referendums in those times. It appears that all governments are prepared to make use of a referendum when they think it can help them to avoid a problem. In the case of the referendum held during the First World War it was a Conservative government that made use of the procedure, and during the Second World War a liberal government made use of it.
To date we have had the experience of the government being sole arbiter as to how, when, and if a referendum will be held. The government is now moving along to create a permanent structure to allow it to proceed in this manner in an easier way.
I am discouraged that the government is not prepared to allow Canadians to voice their opinion concerning the type of question that could be asked. It seems to me the government should be forced to listen to the people because the government wants to consult with Canadians to get itself out of some tight situations.
I am concerned that the present legislation leaves to the government's discretion the question as to who will be able to vote on any referendum it decides to hold. In the present situation the main impetus for this bill is in response to what has happened in Quebec. Just because the Levesque government has stated it will hold a referendum, the federal government appears to want to hold its own referendum in that province. I suggest that it is incorrect for the federal government to impose a referendum on people living in any one region of this country. The federal government, being a national government, should concern itself only with national affairs. If the question of the status and place of Quebec is a national question, then Canadians as a whole should be consulted.
The Minister of Justice, in a statement made earlier this week, has given the impression that any referendum on the status of Quebec in a continuing Canada will be dealt with solely by the population of Quebec. I think this is wrong. This legislation that we are dealing with should be amended at some stage to make it quite clear to everyone that, if the federal government decides to hold a referendum, it would be confined to questions to be dealt with by the entire population of Canada. It is not proper for the federal government to be able to conduct a referendum sponsored by it solely within the confines of Quebec. In my opinion, Canadians generally would like to have something to say about the possible break-up of this country. I would like to be consulted as to the possible future make-up of Canada. I repeat that it is absolutely improper for the federal government to say that it wants to be armed with a tool to allow it to conduct a counter-referendum within the boundaries of one province.
I understand there are some members from the province of Alberta who are concerned that this legislation might be used by the federal government to help it obtain the right to control and direct the development and use of the natural resources of Alberta, and to take over control of their administration. I suppose it is quite possible, the way this bill is framed at the present time, that the federal government could conduct a referendum in the eastern part of Canada asking whether the national government should have complete control over the natural resources of the provinces. In this particular case, whether they said it was all of the provinces, the question would apply primarily to one province, that is, my province of Alberta.
As the Minister of Justice pointed out in his remarks, these are purely consultative votes. They are not binding on anyone. However, this type of procedure could be used in a manner that could create more division than unity in the country. I do not think that is the best argument against this bill. Where a question involves an individual citizen so intimately, there must be provision for that citizen to be consulted. There can be improvements made to this legislation.
I am a little concerned about the statement of the Minister of Justice to the effect that any possible referendum on the future of Quebec will be dealt with only by the citizens of Quebec. That was unfortunate to make that statement before the bill is even passed. At least the minister is honest enough to indicate his feelings. However, it is wrong.
I would like to see the bill amended so that if any question is a national question, every citizen in Canada is entitled to vote on it. If it is not national, the national government does not have any right to ask the question.
I hope consideration will be given to my arguments when this bill goes to committee. The federal government should be prevented from becoming involved in provincial politics. That is not their right. It should stay in its own field, the national field.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in this debate at the second reading stage, but in view of what some newspaper articles may cause Canadians to believe concerning us, as members of the Social Credit Party of Canada, a party which serves indeed as the official Quebec opposition in the Canadian parliament, I feel it is my duty to make a number of observations to clearly define the position of our party and that of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) in respect of Bill C-9.
I listened most attentively to the eloquent remarks the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) made when he introduced this bill. Mr. Speaker, many years ago there was in my riding a great nationalist and a great Canadian, Mr. Armand Lavergne-older members certainly remember him-who made resounding remarks in this House while defending within parliament the rights of Francophone Canadians. And I am happy and proud to represent the same riding. And I would like to follow in those steps, to imitate these shows of strong will, of Canadianism, of nationalism, of support for the development of this country and also to be a great defender of what is contained in the Constitution and which guarantees to the French-speaking people equal rights in their country.
Mr. Speaker, to those members who are relatively young, who perhaps are not familiar with our history of the last decades, of the beginning of the twentieth century, 1 would like to say this: It was during the war of 1914-18 that at a certain point in time, the Canadian government felt that it should take up arms and have Canadians serve in the armed forces and it is then that the conscription act was passed by the parliament and subsequently enforced.
It was under a coalition government that this act was passed and that conscription became compulsory and I remember that Canadians still had the chance to volunteer. I have a brother who volunteered and served overseas for many months, 30 or 32 if I recall, and who fought bravely as all other Canadians did and who at that time believed he was fighting for the course of Christianity, civilization and liberty.
After the war was over, Mr. Speaker, elections were held as they are in our times. I was still very young and I attended one of these political meetings. As we had no parish hall at that time, the meeting was held in the local shoe repair shop. The school building was close by. So, after school, as I already felt a desire to participate in the political life of my country, I went to this meeting and I enjoyed listening to the speeches. Naturally, I was ignorant of those things and I could not pass judgment on all that was said, but my brother who had fought during the war was there. At one point, he challenged the man who was speaking: Stop telling us lies, just tell the truth to these people. I went overseas, I know what happened there and what you are saying now is not true. You must stop this nonsense. The speaker was a brilliant lawyer from Quebec city and he was behaving just like a king in this little town. So he
Referenda
paid no attention to the advice he had been given and he went on. A second time my brother told them. That is enough, just step down from there! He answered back: Nobody is ever going to make me step down. He had hardly said those words that my brother caught him by his tie and took him down. He twisted his tie to the back of his neck and so subdued him, and he had to stop talking. I say this, Mr. Speaker, to show how a battle was started which is still going on today. This is what has brought us to this Bill C-9 respecting public referendums.
Later on, I noticed that during every federal election the same thing happened. This was also involved at the provincial level. Let us remember that Liberals used to tell French Canadians: "Vote for us and you will never be called upon to take part in extraterritorial wars against your will. Vote for us, and conscription will never come to Canada."
Mr. Speaker, it was easy to make that kind of promise when there was no danger of being put to the test. But when the time came to fulfil their commitment, the Liberal government weakened, although on the government side, Liberal members accounted for 99 per cent of members of this House. Then on September 1, 1939 the government proclaimed the War Measures Act and established censorship. Let us make note of the dates: September 1, 1939. The then Prime Minister, Mr. King, called parliament in and stated that were the United Kingdom to declare war, the government had decided that parliament would immediately meet and would be asked to approve efficient co-operation between Canada and Great Britain.
On September 3, Britain declared war. The same day, national defence regulations came into force in Canada. From then on it became a crime to impede recruiting or the success of Her Majesty's forces. Parliament met on September 6. The throne speech referred to the existing state of war. If it were concurred in, the Prime Minister would make a formal war declaration. French Canadian members here in Ottawa en bloc were against Canada's involvement in the war, but they realized that were they to oppose it, the hon. Ernest Lapointe, the then Minister of Justice and the Liberal leader in the province of Quebec, would be forced to resign from cabinet, the result of that resignation being that Prime Minister King would be left in the hands of imperialists, and conscription would shortly follow.
At that time the attitude of French-speaking members was explained in the newspaper Le Devoir by columnist Paul Sauriol.
And they accepted the principle of a moderate participation as the lesser of two evils, as a concession through which conscription could be avoided. Then they changed their mind. They were saying, we are going to participate moderately to avoir conscription. That is what happened later. In the course of debate in this chamber, the hon. Ernest Lapointe made a formidable statement. He said this:

The Quebec premier, Mr. Maurice Duplessis, announced provincial elections for October 25, 1939 ...
I remember the statements made at that time by politicians who were stating on the hustings that it was a scandal to hold elections while the country was at war. Since I have always enjoyed attending political meetings, I have so many memories on that subject.
... alleging a federal invasion of provincial jurisdiction by means of the war measures.
Duplessis was a shrewd man. He would sense that during those war years the provinces, and especially Quebec, would lose part of their autonomy. Events later on bore out his apprehension. With that manoeuvre, Mr. Duplessis thought he could transform an election into a plebiscite which would turn to his own advantage.
On the contrary, the election campaign is dominated by Ernest Lapointe who becomes its real strategist.
He heads the troops at the provincial election level.
Lapointe claims that the federal ministers from Quebec having been attacked by Maurice Duplessis, they would take up the challenge and ask the province of Quebec to give them the needed mark of trust. He does indicate clearly that if Duplessis won, the federal ministers from Quebec would resign and French Canadians would not have any supporters in Ottawa.
How extraordinary it is to see how they played with us. And here, I quote again from Mr. Lapointe's commitments:
And if I recall all those statements, it is to warn us against what could happen if we are not wise, if we rush things, if we try to get around legislative measures in other provinces by way of legislation. I for one prefer to follow the course of events. Before saying "yes" or "no" to a referendum, I want to know the question. That is normal! There was another referendum, in 1942, and I shall talk about that in a moment.
Here is what Mr. Lapointe said at the time, and he was very clear:
I told the English speaking majority in my riding and across the country, frankly, honestly, and squarely: we are going to co-operate, but you have to co-operate also to ensure the unity of Canada-
-we have been hearing of national unity for a long time.
-of the Canadian union, the future of our country... I pay tribute to my English speaking colleagues, to the majority of parliament, who have accepted this offer in a spirit of generosity, and all of parliament is bound by the promise that was made.
So, Mr. Speaker-

So, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government then decided to hold a plebiscite. I am certainly not a linguist, and I have to admit that I do not know the difference between a plebiscite and a referendum. But I look at the aims! And indeed a plebiscite was held in Canada to release the government, Mackenzie King, the Liberal party of the commitments he had made to French Canadians and Francophones in Quebec during many elections. Since those promises had been made to Francophones, it would have been normal that the plebiscite be held only among those whom the promise had been made to. But the plebiscite was held right across Canada. Obviously, Anglophones and Canadians in other provinces readily released Mackenzie King of the promises he had made to French Canadians but Francophones voted a massive "no". However, the government had been released by a majority in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I mention that because there is a direct relationship with Bill C-9. There are excellent things in Bill C-9, the procedures for holding a referendum and all that. It looks very much like the Election Act. That is why in principle the bill is great if it were a legislation to authorize the government and the parliament of Canada to hold the referendum on questions considered important, not on a specific question that concerns only the province of Quebec. That is where, Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with this bill. Of course I will have to oppose it unless the government changes it when it is considered in committee to allow us precisely to agree with a general legislation on referendums, whether it be for the death penalty or another matter of national interest.
We have to remember history. There is a Canadian, the mayor of Montreal, Canada's metropolis, who, like me and many others, believed in the promises of the Liberal party at that time and when that government ordered national registration he felt justified in saying to his fellow citizens: I am not registering because I trust the promise that was made for years. He said: Do not register. And then he was picked up, sent to a concentration camp, kept there during the whole war, without any trial. I find that extraordinary, abominable. There is another Canadian who was sitting at the time in the parliament of Quebec, at the National Assembly. He died recently in the month of December. I am talking about Rene

Chaloult. Another brilliant lawyer, a passionate nationalist. Thanks to him Quebec has its fleur-de-lis flag. I am annoyed, Mr. Speaker, with those young members in the Quebec government who try to make people believe that this has come as a result of some legislation they have passed. It irritates me. I want to point out that he was the one who introduced the motion; then only did the parliament of Quebec, under Mr. Duplessis, pass a bill giving Quebec its fleur-de-lis flag. Things ought to be set out straight, they ought to be reported the way they are. Mr. Speaker, Mr. Chaloult was accused and then prosecuted for having made certain statements, for having repeated things said by Mr. Mackenzie King and others. He brought into court. I have here a booklet which sums up this trial. Fortunately, he was acquitted thanks to the brilliant defense of both his lawyers Fernand Choquette and Phillippe Monette. He was himself a great lawyer. He was able to plead his case while Camilien Houde could not. He did not have the opportunity to do so.
Mr. Speaker, I bring up all these things without any animosity; I would not want people to think that I hold a grudge because I do not, but before we pass this bill, I would like the younger members to look back on our history lest we provide the government with a weapon or a tool for which we could later be sorry. It is our duty to seriously examine the bills that are submitted to parliament, and I hope that at the committee stage, the government will introduce amendments which will revive our confidence in this bill should it ever become law. Since I had said I would be through before five o'clock in order to give someone on the other side the chance to conclude the debate, I shall go no further and I hope that the next speaker will succeed in renewing our confidence.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the House for this privilege. I had really intended to try to answer all the criticisms which have been raised on this bill in order to try to give a general summing up, but in view of the desire of the House to come to a decision I will not engage in that. Instead, what I would like to do is to indicate that a number of points have been raised that we would like to look into a little further. There has been the question of definitions that have been raised, and there has been a question on a number of items, particularly with respect to the question of definition of the constitution which has some members concerned. The definition which we have put into the act was the definition, which is a standard one, which describes the Canadian constitution.
The dilemma we face is that the Canadian constitution is not found in any one document or any one place, it is found in a collection of conventions and legislative enactments. When the decision was taken to allow referenda to be held on the basis of the constitution, we were forced to describe what our constitution was. In the United States, for example, it would be much simpler to describe the constitution, it is contained in a series of documents. Ours is in a series of legislative enact-

ments, bills from the British parliament, as well as a number of statutes which we call constitutional, and that is why that definition is there. If we could find another definition which could describe adequately what our constitution was, we would be prepared to look at it.
The second point I want to raise is the apparent fear that members have about a question being put on the constitutional question, or indeed any kind of question on a referendum. The only answer I can give to that is that elections are divisive, people make choices in elections, parties take stands on particular attitudes and positions, and therefore the fear that has been expressed by a number of members that people would make the wrong decision on a referendum question strikes me as one that I cannot really accept because that is the nature of our democratic society. From that point of view I really cannot find that to be serious.
The second point I want to make before I sit down concerns the question raised by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who said we could use this referendum power to take away the powers of the province, that is, that a province might give up its natural resources through the referendum procedure. Frankly, we have looked at the bill and we cannot find how that kind of charge could be made. The referendum is not binding; it does not bind anyone to anything, which means it has no legal status. It is, as my friend, the hon. member for Westmount (Mr. Johnston), pointed out the other day, a glorified public opinion poll in a way, and therefore has no effect in law at all. Therefore it seems to me that the concerns that people have expressed about the possibility of this referendum taking away powers from the provinces simply do not stand up when one looks at what referenda can do. The hon. member shakes his head. I have listened to his speech and I have read it. He raised this point but he did not express anything except the fear of the question being put and what it might do.
It seems to me to be absurd to assume that the people in my home province of Ontario would vote to give up their natural resources to another province or to the federal government if they did not want to do so, and if they did want to do so, why not use the technique of a referendum to find out? I apologize to the hon. member because I have taken his argument to an absurd ending, but the fact is that the fears that were expressed on this point by hon. members opposite do not seem to bear a relationship to reality.
I want to say also, in answer to my friend who spoke just before me and who said he was interested in the fact that the committee would bring forward amendments, that I recognize that this is a complex bill because what we are doing is to build on to our Election Expenses Act a very complex process. We have taken a different route to that which has been taken in Quebec. We are prepared to look at amendments where necessary changes are to be made and where there are disharmonies in terms of two pieces of legislation, and I trust that members will have an opportunity to make their specific wishes known as soon as possible.
