She said: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the members of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs for their fine co-operation in considering Bill C-2 during almost three working sittings. During those discussions it seemed obvious, I believe, that the decision to anticipate the final date for the expiry of that Canadian legislation which was aimed at the construction, acquisition, renovation and purchase of equipment and buildings for the individual training of health personnel, will not create serious problems concerning production and health manpower in Canada, or the availability of necessary institutions for that purpose.
As for professional and quasi-professional health groups, we now have in Canada a satisfactory level of personnel with adequate training. During the debate on Bill C-2, the major problem raised by opposition members concerned, as I see it, the financing of medical research in Canada. Support for medical research projects is not directly related to the Health Resources Fund programs being terminated sooner than expected by the bill under discussion tonight in the House.
In fact, under the Health Resources Fund Act, more than $100 million have been allocated to planning, construction or purchasing of equipment for research establishments related to training programs. That might be why many opposition members have used this forum to express their points of view and regretfully, I must admit, to criticize our very good work, not so much to criticize the good work but our attitude toward the Medical Research Council of Canada and, generally, the government financial support program for medical research in Canada. May I be allowed to dwell on it a few minutes.
The Medical Research Council, which is the main institution in Canada granting subsidies for medical research, is under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It is a Crown agency which is distinct from my department and which has its own budget of over $60 million to which is added indirectly, through a specific program of my department, a budget of close to $10 million coming from what the government gives, what the federal government gives back for medical research from taxpayers monies. Those government subsidies amount to some 50 per cent of all subsidies given to that sector in Canada, the other 50 per cent coming mainly from the private sector, from associations like the Canadian Heart Foundation, the Canadian Cancer Society, the association for arthritis and so on, and for a few years, from small but well appreciated amounts given by some provincial governments. I consider that there will perhaps never be enough funds for medical research in Canada, and I
February 1, 1979

understand in this regard the constructive criticism which could be made to ensure funding. It will always be possible to increase the portion which is directed to medical research. But I fail to understand why the government is being criticized, rightly or wrongly, for not having done its part, because medical research is one of its priorities and will remain so.
The last positive decision dealing with biomedical researchers in Canada is the one the cabinet made to allow long-term financing, or in other words, guarantee the stability, of the Medical Research Council funding. A request to that effect had been made a long time ago. As a matter of fact, I believe it was made three years ago. It takes into account the fact that according to public opinion Canadians are eager to see medical research improved in Canada.
Therefore, before Christmas, I was able to announce a formula for determining the annual level of expenditures for the Medical Research Council from 1978 to 1983. It is noted that this five-year stabilization formula is absolutely unique as no government likes to commit itself ahead of time with one of its departments or agencies. Still, with the support of my colleagues, I made the point that the very nature of medical research requires that researchers know in advance where they are going, because the average project lasts three years, and because the money we give the Medical Research Council is used mainly to create jobs for technicians and one or two researchers who at times lead the teams. Jobs and people are therefore involved and I felt it was urgent that they be given some guarantee of stability with regard to the funds granted by the government. The present budget, therefore, amounts to exactly $63,002,000.
With the new formula, the basic budget of the council will now be figured out every year by adding to the current funds the increase in the cost of living index, plus the percentage of actual growth of our GNP, less one per cent. This calculation is intended to counter inflationary pressures that might build up within the system itself. Application of this formula, as approved by the cabinet, will mean a subsidy of $68.8 million will be paid to the Medical Research Council for the fiscal year 1979-80.
I indicated that this formula would be used to calculate the basic budget of the council, but another aspect of the government's decision is to favourably consider any application for additional funding, over and above this basic budget, which the council would submit to us for specific programs or priorities, for new and major projects aimed at upgrading the health of Canadians. Of course, the council is already funding many projects of a national scope. For instance, in 1977-78, it provided more than $3 million for research and training of researchers in the area of respiratory diseases. It provided more than $6 million for research on cancer and an equal amount on cardiovascular disorders. In the current year, the
Health Resources Fund Act
council is giving special encouragement to the expansion of research centres in cardiology. This explains the new programs in Winnipeg and Halifax. To the budget currently allowed to the council will be added, if need be, new proposals that will come from the scientific community.
The new budgetary provisions for the Medical Research Council will give assurance to those health professional schools in which the biomedical research effort has not yet achieved a solid base so that developmental funds would be available for the recruitment and support of additional faculty members competent in research. It is necessary that each such school have a research base with some depth as well as breadth so that its students will receive professional education which is up to date and the patients in the region will receive treatment which is also up to date. This development grant program has been a priority for the council as it has been for the government for many years. It is paying off, and its momentun can now be maintained without encroaching on the funds required for the maintenance of other efforts. With the new funding the number of highly qualified young investigators who can expect to receive salary support from the council as they develop independent research programs can be maintained at a level considered adequate to meet the demands of those who will also be assured of research funding.
These young scholars and their counterparts supported by the council under other programs may also look forward to a narrowing of the gap in 1979-80 between the salary provided by the Medical Research Council and the university salary provided to their academic colleagues. A slightly larger number of awards for research trainees will be available in the coming year than were awarded this year. Furthermore, the stipends attached to these awards are to be increased to offset somewhat higher living costs. This will be particularly welcome to those who are taking advanced training in centres outside Canada.
The greatest benefit to the research community to arise from the introduction of that new basic formula funding will, however, be felt by the investigators across the country who receive operating funds for their research from the Medical Research Council. The budget now proposed for the council and approved by the cabinet will provide for increases in ongoing grants which are more commensurate with the cost increases of research materials and supplies and the salary increases of the technicians and other assistants who are paid from these grants.
Investigators have in the past complained that on occasion they could only make ends meet by dispensing with the services of a technician. I am not sure of the extent to which that can be documented, but it is certainly true that biomedical research is a labour-intensive industry. I would like to impress on the public that fact, which is not known at all. I suppose if we were discussing this matter with neighbours or with people in shopping centres, they would think more is

February 1, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
spent on equipment, including monkeys and experimental animals, but each dollar we give to biomedical research through the grants of the council in fact helps support jobs, basically technicians' jobs. Some 65 per cent of the expenditures by the Medical Research Council grantees are for the payment of technical or other assistants or research trainees. With the proposed budget the president of the Medical Research Council has estimated that instead of jobs being lost, at least 100 more jobs will now be created. A formula based on economic indicators should serve to eliminate the stop-go effect on the biomedical research effort which has been the result of pressures in recent years created in part by inflation and in part by the increasing numbers of well trained young scientists seeking to establish research projects in our universities or hospitals.
Supporting even a minimal number of these young scientists and their research has in some years meant the interruption, if not the disruption, of research by investigators of long standing. Even with the new formula it will probably not be possible to support the research of all those who, in the opinion of their peers, are doing creditable work. However, combined with the realistic forward planning which this formula will permit-I want to repeat that the formula is a five-year funding mechanism-the new formula should ensure that well qualified young men and women with new ideas and new techniques and established investigators of longer experience are on an equal footing in the competition for research funds.
During the standing committee's study of Bill C-2 statements were made by a member of the opposition that the government's decision on the new funding formula for the Medical Research Council had not been well received by the research community. I am very pleased to see that gentleman in the House tonight and I would like to take this opportunity to answer that charge, to state strongly that I disagree with him and to say that, on the contrary, the new formula has been very well received by the Medical Research Council which is comprised largely of well-known Canadian scientists. I should also like to say that all the correspondence received by both Dr. Simard, the president of the Medical Research Council, and by myself reveals a very positive response on the part of senior and responsible members of the scientific community, among them, if I can name only one from my own city, being Dr. Charles Scriver, who appeared on two occasions as a witness at the invitation of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to plead the case for stable funding.
Of course, this new five year plan will not, nor is it expected to, eliminate all the problems linked with biomedical research. It should, however, restore a degree of stability to the research effort which is essential if we are to make the best possible use of our resources.
If I go back to the exact nature of this bill, which is to cancel the health resources fund a few years ahead of its natural termination date, I must acknowledge that many members complained in the committee about the fact that no

consultation had taken place with the provinces on introducing an earlier cut-off date after which no new projects are to be approved. The fact is that there was very little time for specific consultation when the final decision was taken. However, given the state of the economy, given the federal-provincial conference of first ministers in 1978, this program, as I explained in committee, was obviously a prime candidate for cuts because the fund had given most of what it could give to Canada. Provinces were informed of the proposed change by telex on September 8, 1978. They were also told that we would fully honour the commitment on projects approved to date. This program is not one with any formal federal-provincial agreement. Hon. members will remember that it was established by a law of this parliament in 1966 to enable the provinces to more rapidly develop health research and training facilities, and it has been successful in meeting this target. There was a need to curtail certain levels of planned expenditures in current and future department budgets for which I am responsible, and this decision was conveyed to the provinces. [Translation]
When the Health Resources Fund was established in 1966, Canada had 12 schools of medicine and 880 doctors who graduated that same year. There was a ratio of one active doctor for 762 people. Compared to the most recent statistics for 1977 we realize that there are now 16 schools of medicine training twice as many physicians. There is now a ratio of two active civilian physicians for 568 people. When I say active civilian physicians I include in my definition general practitioners, family physicians and all specialists. New specialties have also appeared in Canada in recent years particularly in the field of rehabilitation, ergotherapy, cardiovascular surgery, pediatric surgery, nuclear medicine and cancer treatment medicine. Because of this, hospital environments have become extremely complex bioscientific centres where clinical research is always accompanied by highly specialized therapy.
A detailed study on the need for doctors in Canada by medical specialties was undertaken in 1972 at the cost of more than $300,000 by the federal government. The report on this vast research, which was published in 1975, shows that even though the specialist distribution by specialty is not always adequate and the geographic distribution could be better, the total number of doctors in Canada should not necessarily be increased.
Indeed, the ratio recommended by the members of Canadian medical associations associated with the study is one doctor for 670 people, which excludes interns and residents. If we consider that the latter represent about 15 per cent of the total number of doctors, we reach a figure of one doctor for 566 inhabitants. The fear of seeing an excessive production threaten the balance of medical staff has brought about a drastic reduction in the immigration of doctors through restrictive regulations which have caused a decrease in the number of doctors immigrating to Canada from 1,000 a year in previous years to a little over 300 a year in the last few years. Of

course, this is a strict minimum if we want to admit refugees and the spouses of immigrants.
Our medical schools now produce 1,700 graduates a year in Canada. This figure is quite sufficient, and we must realize that if we had to increase it, our present schools have a maximum capacity of 2,500 students. This is based on a study made in 1973 by Dr. Rocke Robertson.
It seems absurd at this point in time to insist in the short term on increasing the productivity of our medical schools, or even expanding our postgraduate training programs. Our present efforts are directed at attracting professionals towards outlying areas where service is poor as well as towards the specialities which are most in demand, and this is being done by joint task forces composed of provincial representatives as well as spokesmen for professional associations and officials from my department.

Since the onset of the health resources fund, the manpower ratio for all disciplines in health has shown continued improvement. For example, the number of health professionals and paraprofessionals in relation to population shows a substantial positive change for the eight year period from 1968 to 1976.1 should like to refer to a few examples.
In 1968, the ratio was one physician for every 740 people, whereas the ratio in 1976 was one for every 578 people. The ratio in respect of nurses was one for every 187 Canadians in 1968; whereas in 1976 the ratio was one for every 129 Canadians. The list continues, but I will not take the time of the House giving further examples.
In the dental field, the number of dental schools increased from six to ten, bringing the output of graduates from 296 in 1966 to 465 in 1976. New dental schools were constructed with health resources fund assistance at Universite Laval, Quebec; the University of Western Ontario, London, Ontario; the University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; and the University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia. Substantial assistance was approved to expand and improve facilities at Dalhousie University in Halifax and at the University of Manitoba in Winnipeg. The ratio of dentists to population improved from one per 3,097 Canadians in 1966 to one per 2,438 in 1976. Also, the significant improvement in numbers of graduates for other dental personnel is noteworthy. Dental assistant graduates numbered 58 in 1966 and increased to 917 in 1978. For dental hygienists, it was 82 in 1966 as compared to 350 in 1976. Due to market and employment conditions, some provinces are reducing the number of student enrolments in the dental auxiliary field.
In the nursing field, we witnessed the transfer of didactic training programs for nurses from the hospital to the formal educational setting, primarily in CEGEP and community colleges. Similarly, the period of training for diploma nurse graduates was reduced in most instances from a three-year hospital program to a two-year community college program. The number of graduates increased from 7,387 in 1966 to
Health Resources Fund Act
10,051 in 1976. As I have said, the ratio has improved remarkably. One can even say that Canada has an over-supply of nurses and almost the highest ratio of nurses to population in the world. We have adequate facilities for the training of physicians, dentists, nurses and most other health disciplines. In fact, there is a trend toward a levelling off of new trainees accepted in our training schools, and, in some instances, a reduction policy is being implemented. As a result we now have a surplus of nurses and an acceptable doctor to population ratio. The ratios for all other disciplines have improved and will continue to improve in relation to economic and social requirements.
On the international level, our manpower ratios compare favourably with a number of other countries. The ratio of physicians in Canada in 1974 was better or equal to those of Australia, the United States, England, Wales, Scotland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, Netherlands, Luxembourg, France, Spain and Portugal. We were surpassed moderately by Belgium, Italy, West Germany, Switzerland and the U.S.S.R. As for dentists, Canada fared better than England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Scotland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Spain, and Australia. Only Australia, the United States, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Finland, France, West Germany, Switzerland and the U.S.S.R. had better ratios. As for nurses, Canada had a better ratio than all countries mentioned except Denmark.
During the 1966-1978 period, the health resources fund met the objective of having the necessary facilities on a national basis to train health personnel in sufficient numbers to meet the current and anticipated demands. For example, our medical schools have levelled off in the number of trainees accepted and some are operating below potential capacity. Recently a great number of projects approved under the fund have been to assist with the expansion and upgrading of teaching hospitals. With the trend now toward a reduction in training in these institutions, this type of requirement has diminished.
In the last 30 years, and to a greater extent in the last ten years, there has been rapid and substantial development of training and other health facilities all over Canada. There will be a need, to a much lesser degree, to maintain and upgrade existing schools and related facilities which in most instances are new or renovated structures. There will not be the demand for large injections of capital in this area, nor increases in the enrolment of trainees in the health field. It is for these reasons that Bill C-2 is before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I was surprised at the tone of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). In the last half of her remarks she seemed to indicate she was quite satisfied that everything in the health field is well, nothing further needed to be done, and therefore the health resources fund can be chopped easily without any detrimental results. Perhaps this indicates the minister's lack of appreciation for the health field and her complete disinterest in it. If the minister had bothered to

Health Resources Fund Act
inform herself fully on the problems in the health field, certainly she would not have taken the attitude she did.
The minister began her comments by criticizing my party for having spoken on medical research during consideration of this bill. Then she proceeded to spend at least 20 minutes speaking on medical research. In addition, she was somewhat dishonest when she accused us of criticizing the Medical Research Council. I challenge her to show examples in Hansard or the minutes of committee proceedings of my party criticizing the Medical Research Council. That was a blatant dishonesty on her part. We criticized the minister's policy of starving the Medical Research Council to death in its attempt to fund research in the country. Our criticism has been levelled always at the minister and her government, not at the Medical Research Council.

The minister went on at some length to indicate that the health resources fund had nothing to do with research, and that we were abusing the bill in talking about research. Yet, I have in my possession a sessional paper dated March 10, 1978, which was signed by the minister. I am referring to sessional paper 303-1/156 in which the Health Resources fund is discussed.
In this paper it indicates quite clearly that $75 million has been allocated for the support of health training and research projects of national significance. I do not see how the minister can stand up and state with a straight face that the health resources fund has nothing to do with research, because her own paper signed in her own hand indicates that $75 million of that fund was indeed channeled toward research of national significance.
We have opposed this bill primarily for two reasons. One reason is the high-handed method the government used to introduce the legislation and its failure to consult with the provinces. It was a unilateral decision with an announcement to the press, followed five days later by a telex to the provincial health ministers informing them that the fund would be terminated.
The other reason we opposed this bill was its detrimental effect on research, by cutting off funds for medical research to an even greater degree than she and her predecessors have done over the past decade.
We learned some interesting facts, however, about the minister and this government during debate on this bill. I think the Toronto Star article of January 27 describes what we learned quite clearly. The headline reads, "Boss Begin's in Trouble. Lack of Leadership has Staff near Mutiny". In reading through this article it clearly indicates why the minister has been so erratic during the debate and why she seems to have flip-flopped at least four or five times on various issues over the past three months. The article is based on information gained from talking to a senior civil servant and perhaps other officials who are close to her. It describes the minister as
insecure, and floundering under her scatter gun approach and indecisive dodging. We saw examples of that in her comments earlier. The article goes on to say that it is not easy for a civil servant working with a minister who is so nervous that she specifically ordered senior officials not to discuss her. I do not think I will spend any more time with this article. Anybody wishing to see it can look it up for himself.

I would like to continue my comments if I could. In her opening comments, when this bill was presented for second reading, the minister indicated her philosophy and that of the government on programs which they have had in place for a number of years. With regard to the health resources fund, the essence of what the minister said at that time is that it was a terrific program, and that, therefore, the government decided to scrap it. The comment took me by surprise, because if you have a good program it is natural to want to continue it and perhaps even expand on it. My party's philosophy is that if a good program is in effect you do not scrap it, you keep it, because it is usually the best in terms of serving the public.

February 1, 1979

In spite of the self-righteous attitude of the minister with regard to the trained personnel available in this country, she is far from correct. For example, Canada has almost no specialists in the Field of geriatrics. This is a very rapidly growing field, and as our population ages and the birth rate drops over the next two decades, it will continue to grow. However, there seems to be no attention whatever paid to this area in the minister's comments.
The minister was proud of the fact that the nurses training program had been reduced from three years in a hospital to two years in a community college. In my opinion, and that is all it is, that program has been a step backward because it has resulted in less qualified individuals providing nursing services. I would suggest that the three-year program be reinstated because that extra year is necessary to instil the proper "Florence Nightingale" attitude in the minds of the young ladies who wish to serve their fellow man in that particular field.
The minister's behaviour during this debate has been rather erratic. The bill originally announced an $84 million cut from the health resources fund, but within just a couple of weeks or a month of the commencement of public debate on the bill, and as a result of the criticism it received, the minister reversed her decision and added $15 million to the pot. 1 do not criticize her for that move, because I think it was a good one. What I am questioning is why she would announce something and reverse her decision just three or four weeks after the matter became public. Whether it was because it was a bad decision to begin with or because she was not completely informed of what was happening, I do not know. I would say it indicates she made a bad decision, that when the pressure was put on by the public and by this side of the House she caved in and changed her mind in order to reduce that pressure.

speechtext: She sounds like Joe Clark.

I suppose that the New Democrats will have a speaker to put forth their position in a few moments, but I will not waste too much of my time on them.
There have also been charges from this side of the House that the bill was introduced without consultation with the provinces.
For a long time the minister insisted during debate in this House and in committee that there was consultation with the provinces. She was defended in that position by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet). He attacked us very vigorously for being "unfair" and saying things that were "untrue" when we accused her of taking unilateral action and bringing in this bill which affected the provinces directly without having first consulted them. A reading of page 1599 of Hansard for November 28, 1978, would indicate that the Minister of State for Urban Affairs went to some lengths to try to convince the House that there was plenty of consultation with the provinces.
Health Resources Fund Act
When the bill went to committee, the minister again reversed herself. In the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs of December 12, 1978, at page 7:21, the minister said:
You want a simple answer, why were the provincial ministers not consulted on my cuts, because they are not elected in the federal portfolio; they have no accountability whatsoever of my budget to any Canadian voter and I really resent the suggestion of the member.
After all that defence, she then admitted that she did not consult the provinces. When we pursued the question of why not, she said in essence that she did not have to, that it was strictly a federal program and the provinces did not have to be consulted. Earlier on the same day, referring to a particular research fund, she said, at page 7:8:
Our national economy is a tight economy, so are the economies of the provinces, and this program is by definition a fifty-fifty venture.
This leads us to wonder where the minister really stands. On the one hand she says the provinces were not consulted because this is strictly a federal program and is none of their business, so to speak, but on the same day she says this program is "by definition a fifty-fifty venture."
It is no wonder that the Toronto Star ran an article on January 27 criticizing the minister's lack of leadership. Whoever it was that the reporter talked to in her department or on her staff said that the department is floundering under her scatter gun approach. These examples indicate why the minister has not been able to do the job that was expected of her.
We criticize this bill on the basis that it has a devastating effect on research. The budget for the Medical Research Council was announced in the usual manner in the blue book. Later, as a result of pressure from the research community and from this side of the House, an additional $2 million was allocated to meet its needs. Six to eight weeks later, however, half a million dollar was subtracted. We then had a situation in which the Medical Research Council, which is largely responsible for medical research in this country, was faced with three different budgets in one year. First of all, the blue book budget, then an additional $2 million, and then a decrease of half a million. I cannot think of a better example of erratic behaviour than that.
The research budget has been eroded very substantially over the past few years. It is true that on this side of the House we have urged the government for a number of years to implement a formula of stable, long-term funding for research over a three-year or five-year period which would enable research organizations to engage in proper planning.
We did not criticize the minister for committing herself to the principle of a long-term funding formula as she seemed to suggest we did; what we criticized was the content of the formula which commits the government of funding the Medical Research Council for a five-year period with increments based on the implicit price index. In essence, this means increases of about 11 per cent per year. We know from the experts in the research community that the inflation rate in research-the increased costs in research-runs from 15 per cent to 17 per cent per year. It therefore becomes obvious that

February 1, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
this formula, which increases funding by 11 per cent, will not even keep up to this year's level of funding and that each year thereafter there will be a loss of about 6 per cent. In essence, the government has committed itself to a 6 per cent per year erosion in the Medical Research Council funding for the next five years. If this formula had been applied to the last six years or so the budget this year would have been about $7 million less than it is.
While we support the principle of a long-term formula for funding, the formula itself is somewhat of a joke. It will create greater difficulties for research than have been experienced thus far.
I want to touch briefly on another matter, Mr. Speaker, and that is the Indian health service guidelines which were implemented only a few weeks ago. The minister indicated that she felt the Indian people as a whole were abusing the health care services that were provided. I want to object to that sort of criticism because I do not see why that particular group of people should be singled out. It is quite easy to see that some people in every group in society are abusing the health care system to some extent, and I can give a specific example of that.
I do some part-time work in one of the emergency departments of a local hospital, Mr. Speaker. Each patient who walks in there automatically costs the taxpayer $21 in hospital costs plus $15 or so for the medical service that is provided. If that patient went to see a doctor in his office the $21 emergency hospital cost would be saved. Yet we see hundreds of people from all walks of life in the emergency departments of this country every day. They complain of things like sore throats, runny ears, coughs of two or three weeks' duration, skin rashes, aches and pains-in fact, all the normal things seen by a general practitioner in his office. All kinds of people go to the emergency department, a very expensive place to dispense these simple medical services.
If the minister is concerned about anybody abusing the medical services in this country, she should not single out the weakest group in our society, the Indian people. She should look at everybody else, including herself, perhaps.
It any case, Mr. Speaker, the minister made the accusation and brought in guidelines which resulted in some dangerous reductions in health services. They meant cutting back on prescription drugs, for instance. It is easy to imagine what the effect would be on a diabetic patient who needed insulin, could not pay for it, and the new guidelines perhaps would not allow him to get it free. The patient could be in a coma within 24 hours.
Another important service is the ambulance service. There may be some abuses here, but it is not just the Indian people who are responsible. If there were a genuine need for an ambulance, because someone was unconscious or in great pain, the ambulance driver would make a quick judgment as to whether the trip was necessary. But, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that most ambulance drivers are not trained to make such judgments. This puts everybody in a difficult position.

As a result of pressure from the Indian people and from this side of the House the minister reversed her decision. She delayed the guidelines for six months. We criticized her because she imposed the guidelines without first consulting the Indian people. We took the position that if they were abusing the services, as she said, the proper thing to do would be to go to their councils and discuss the problem, pointing out where the abuses occur and where corrective action could be taken. She decided not to do that. The minister did not want to talk to them, she just cut off the service. But when the outcry came she had to reverse her decision. Why did she announce something which she later had to renounce? Why did she not consult with the people directly in the first place? Was this a bad decision; was she uninformed or was she given bad advice-what was it? Whatever it was it suggests to me that the department, insofar as her authority is concerned, is not being run very smoothly or in the interest of the country. The decision was reversed and the minister has said she will take six months to consult with the Indian people. Why was this not done before?
I had some serious reservations about the actions of this minister which were elicited during the debate on this bill. I put them before the House but I do not expect the government to take any action-it never does. Nevertheless, it is on the record and I hope the next minister of health will try to do a better job in the interests of Canadians.

who spoke before me. These were not the thoughts I had when I was getting ready to say a few words on this bill. After his speech I felt that something like this should be said.

I do not agree. I am an unrepentant federalist. I am a Canadian. I like to see standards of living and standards of health maintained at the same high level right across Canada. Mr. Speaker, some members are probably wondering why an agrologist is getting up to speak on health care. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is no doubt worried that I may talk about the health of animals and brucellosis. I am tempted to do that, but I know it would be out of order.
I wish to make a few comments tonight with regard to two areas. First, I will plead the case for more research in the health area for native people. I will deal with a number of statistics that are somewhat appalling when comparing native people and non-native people in this country.
I would also like to speak briefly about health resources funds being used to help young graduates attain a higher level of education by providing them with more funds. This is very necessary in the realm of education today. Many students attend university and receive their bachelor of science degrees, bachelor of arts degrees, or whatever. They then Find that salaries are so attractive it would be too much for them to continue in their education. Therefore, we are not getting the numbers of young people continuing on to a masters or a doctors degree that will be required. This is because they are not being adequately supported by the governments of the day.
It was pointed out today that the Agriculture Institute of Canada is very worried about the fact that not enough students are continuing in their education to become the scientists of tomorrow. This particular funding is being provided in the health field, but governments should take this as a warning and provide funding in other fields as well.
I can give the example of CIDA. Non-Canadians are brought to this country to attend our universities. They are helped with the cost of their training. Hopefully they will return to their countries after completing their education. These students are provided with sufficient funding that they receive incomes of upwards of $6,000. In addition, their rooms, food and tuition are taken care of. Therefore, they can come to Canada and get their masters or doctors degree with relative ease.
Our graduate students are not accommodated in the same way by the Canadian government. As a result, they are looking for high paying jobs rather than becoming our much needed scientists of tomorrow. I thought I would comment on that because I am worried about my faculty and the research capability that will be available in the future as a result of this important situation.
An area that concerns me more is native health care in this country. The hon. member for Athabasca stated that $75 million of this health resource fund was spent on health research. It is my plea tonight that more funds be made available for the health research area. If they can be found, they should be channelled toward native health research and native health development. The statistics that I read trouble me. I intend to put them on the record. Much of the funding is channelled to health care that will help everyone, but not enough is being channelled to the area of native health development.

The minister recently announced some cutbacks in noninsured areas. The native people were so concerned that some 2,500 of them marched on the federal buildings in Edmonton, Alberta. The maritime chiefs found it necessary to come here to meet with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in order to discuss this.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) pointed out that the cost of moving Indian affairs personnel across the river from Ottawa to Hull cost $6 million, of which $500,000 was expended on the actual move. Money is still being spent on the accommodation in Ottawa that was vacated. Some of that funding could be provided for the research and development that is necessary to eliminate some of those areas in respect of Indian health care where these people are not being cared for adequately.
Bill C-2 is a cutback bill in the area of health services. The concept of health, if it is to be meaningful, must be viewed in the broadest possible context. This context must encompass the physical and social aspects of a person's well-being. It cannot refer only to the absence of disease. Indian people do not enjoy the state of health enjoyed by other Canadians. This is revealed most dramatically by statistics. The statistics with respect to the health of the Indian people in my province are horrifying. In Alberta the greatest causes of death among Indians are accidents, violence and poisoning. Dr. Kirkbride, the regional director of the Alberta Region, stated in his address to the All-Indian Chief Conference that accidents and violence accounted for 69 male and 30 female deaths. This represented some 37 per cent of all deaths among registered Indians. Many of these deaths were alcohol-related and could have been prevented. They were useless deaths. Violence accounted for most of the deaths occurring among those in the age group one to 49. Fifty-six out of every 100 deaths in pre-school children are due to accidents and violence. Sixty-six out of every 100 deaths in school children aged five to 14 are due to accidents and violence. Seventy-seven out of every 100 deaths among young adults aged 15 to 29 are due to accidents and violence.
The statistics on child mortality rates are just as frightening. The infant mortality rate per thousand live births for Indian people in Alberta in 1963 was 5.7. In 1970 it was 4.1 and in 1977 it was 2.2. One might say that the statistics show a drop and this is good to see, but it is still much higher than the 1.6 non-Indian infant mortality rate in 1977-1.6 as compared with 2.2 represents a difference of almost 60 per cent. When we look at the national statistics we find the mortality rate for Indian children is 2.4 per thousand compared to a national average among non-native children of 1.6.
I have just one more statistic concerning the average age of death to put on record, Mr. Speaker. It concerns the rate for adults. The average age of male deaths in Canada for the year 1973 was 63.6. For females it was 69.1. If we look at the average age for Canadian Indian males we find it was 41.5 in 1973 and 43.3 for females. In Alberta the statistics were even
February 1, 1979

more alarming. The average age of death for Alberta Indians in 1973 was 37.4 years of age for females and 39.7 for males. This is astonishing and is one of the reasons why I feel compelled to plead this case tonight. I plead for more funds to be made available out of the Health Resources Fund than the $75 million which was available under these provisions and which would be to cut off under the terms of the bill before us.
Why are the native peoples living 23 or 24 years less than we are? If we consider some diseases, for instance, tuberculosis, which most of us do not even think about any more, we find they are on the increase among native people. I only have the statistics for Alberta but in that province there were 75 cases of TB in 1973 among native people. It has not significantly decreased, since the 1977 figure of 67. Treaty Indians in the northern part of the province experienced no incidence of TB ten years ago but in 1975 there were 18 cases and in 1977, 21 cases were reported. These statistics are an alarming indication of the over-all state of health suffered by the native people in this country. I could give many more examples because the Alberta Indian Association came to see me last week and left me some 100 pages documenting the proposition that their health care in non-insured areas should not be cut back.
As I said earlier, we need a broad definition of health. Therefore when considering the issue of poor health among Indians we must regard the socioeconomic conditions in which Indian people live. This encompasses a broad range of matters such as housing, sanitation, recreation, nutrition and employment. If one considers the issue of infant mortality, for example, the general level of sanitation in Indian communities would certainly affect the well-being of infants and children.
I would like here to quote Dr. Lyle Black, a senior official in the Ministry of National Health and Welfare. He is in charge of medical care for Indians and he said that he would not drink the water on the majority of the reserves in Canada today because of the lamentable sanitary and health conditions to be found there. He said that clean water, properly heated, insulated houses and recreation facilities all contribute to a child's health and well-being.
Again, we can refer to the need for good nutrition. It is well known that poor nutrition has long been a major contributing factor to lowered mental functioning, greater susceptibility to infectious diseases, poor oral hygiene and vision problems. Health problems such as gall bladder infection, infectious diseases, high infant mortality, nutritional anaemia, obesity, retarded physical growth, are increasingly plaguing our Indian people in this country today.
Ray Obomsawin, the health co-ordinator with the National Indian Brotherhood, stated in a 1977 paper that the incidence of diabetes among Indians was five times higher than among the general population. Yet one of the guidelines the minister announced would mean doing away with prescription drugs. We see the necessity of these drugs being available to the Indian people when we look at statistics like the diabetes statistics to which I have just referred.
Health Resources Fund Act
I have noted that the main causes of death among Indians are accidents, violence and poisonings. For example, I will refer to the Hobbema Reserve in my own constituency. The Globe and Mail-an eastern paper but I was glad to note their interest in the subject-reported that people on this reserve were killing themselves at a rate 20 times greater than the national average. The community nurse in charge noted that during an 18-month period ending October, 1977, in addition to the 17 reported suicides there were 21 deaths due to consistent abuse in the use of alcohol and drugs. Seven people were found dead in unusual circumstances, although crime could not be proven. Seven deaths occurred in car accidents and four deaths among infants were due at least partially to neglect. There were four infant and 21 adult deaths due to natural causes. These facts are appalling and I cite them to illustrate the seriousness of the problem faced by the Indian people.
The reserve in my constituency to which I refer is one of the better-off Alberta reserves. There are oil revenues which provide much opportunity, and everything possible is being done to remedy this problem. Two detoxification centres have been established. They are being run by native people, and they are very successful. Attempts are being made to find employment for most of the people on the reserve. Still, we see statistics about people dying because of conditions under which other people do not have to live. That is why trained people who understand the problem are needed to work in consultation with native people to learn the reasons for these problems. Perhaps in this way they can be solved and conditions for native people can be brought closer to the national average.
I wanted to talk about problems regarding noon hour lunches for native Indian children, a policy which was discontinued. However, I will leave that for another time.
It is important that we improve conditions, and I have talked about that in my speech. There are complex problems, but we must consider prevention, research, community involvement and a high level of co-ordination and co-operation on the part of all groups and organizations concerned about the health of Indians.
To date this government has demonstrated that it lacks consistency and that it lacks co-ordination between departments. One department throws up its hands and says a certain problem is not its responsibility. There is no consistent, unified policy regarding Indian health. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has said, and I quote:
I also recognize that the statistics on health show Indian people generally to be below the Canadian average. However, the basic causes for this are socio-economic, for example, inadequate housing, water supply and sewage disposal and unemployment.
The minister went on to say:
These matters are outside the control of my department.
I am happy that the minister realizes there are problems in those areas, but she should not throw up her hands, say that they are outside the control of her department and slough the

February 1, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
problems off on someone else. It happens too often when people come to departments for help, that departments tell them their problems are not the responsibilities of those departments and that they should go somewhere else.
Then there are cutbacks, and the minister says they are not her responsibility. Surely the minister should have consulted the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) as well as native people. She should have consulted the Alberta Indian association, the Canadian Indian association and perhaps even some bands to decide whether more research funds should be spent.
I talked about consultation. There is to be a six-month period of grace. The National Indian Brotherhood has emphasized the need for involvement of tribal and band governments in the process of clearly defining health goals. Indian people know very well that they should be involved at all stages of negotiation and planning with regard to native programs. They should be involved from the community level up. Indian problems differ from those of the non-native community.
Another area of concern to me is the need for preventive health care. I want to quote Dr. Lyle Black, director-general of medical services, who has said that a shortcoming in the area of medical services "was apparently a total lack of programs related to preventive health".
Dr. Black said further that co-ordination between all government and university health services is needed to reduce the basic unsanitary and unhygienic conditions which can range from house design and house construction to water supply systems and waste water disposal systems which are rendered particularly difficult by such things as permafrost. Dr. Black also mentioned, something which we as non-native people do not experience, that many doctors and nurses who go into native communities, which are often far away from civilization, are not prepared to spend much time there. Because of that, many native people go to their doctor, are examined, subjected to tests and released, only to return a few weeks later when their problems still are not solved to find there is a new doctor who orders new tests and new prescriptions. The poor patients do not know where they stand. Dr. Black emphasized that the Department of National Health and Welfare should consider it obligatory that doctors who go into these areas keep very extensive notes on the problems of patients so that if there is a turnover, doctors who come in as replacements know exactly what treatment should be given, what tests have been done and what the results of those tests are.
I wanted to make a case tonight not only for the Indian and native people in my riding but also for those all across Canada. I hope the Department of National Health and Welfare will take into account the statistics which have been put on the record and the need for adequate research into why these statistics are as they are. I hope the department will attempt to solve this problem and bring the health of native people up to the same standard as that enjoyed by other Canadians.
The minister said she reversed herself when she offered a six-month grace period with regard to cutbacks. I think it is very important that after six months the cutbacks are not just
re-introduced, with nothing happening in the meantime. It is very important that the consultation process go on, that native people be taken into consideration and that the health care of this very important group in our society is adequate.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief comments on Bill C-2 which strikes me as being of capital importance. Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Health Resources Fund Act, chapter H-4 of our statutes. The act stipulated that payments be made to help the provinces finance medical research with a view to improving the health of Canadians. Bill C-2 says, and I quote:
No payment shall be made under this Act in respect of any cost incurred in respect of a health training facility unless payment of a contribution toward the cost thereof was authorized by the Minister pursuant to subsection 4(1) or 5(1) before September 9,1978."
I agree wholeheartedly with the earlier comments of the House leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am convinced he was sincere when he said the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) was doing everything she could to improve research possibilities and give Canadians a chance to improve their condition and their health. Unfortunately he added-and it is with a little regret that I express this reservation with respect to Bill C-2 because I believe that in 1979 the best investment we could make would be to continue to provide assistance for research to allow our institutions to provide better health services.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because I happen to have a daughter who is in that field and who loves her work very much. She was telling me at Christmas that she deplores that our hospitals could not do more precisely because of those restrictions and the lack of financial resources.
There may be cases sometimes, Mr. Speaker, where money, taxes paid by Canadians are being misused. That does not give the results we would like to see. But considering the percentage of waste that may exist, I do believe that the government should not reduce the funds intended for research because in the final analysis the people of Canada are living in an excessively difficult climate. I sometimes compare our conditions here in Canada with those in some other countries, particularly during the difficult months we are going through. We had a very tough month of January. We had big snowstorms. It was cold. We had difficult climatic conditions. In spite of all that, I say it is one of the attractive features of Canada that countries like those in the far south do not experience.
But we have to be prepared for that. We need very well designed houses, particularly these days, because of concerns with respect to energy reserves. We need well-insulated houses. However, I find complaining all the time a little disgusting and sometimes disheartening because you have to recognize that

we have certain advantages in Canada in spite of the climate and the harsh winters. Today is February 1. Tonight we realized that the sun set a little later, so the day was longer, the sun was out longer, and it seems to me that every day we are going to gain vitality.

I do not participate in these debates anticipating that we will necessarily receive the correct answer. In reply to the hon. member's interjection, quite often we receive no answer at all.
The Minister of Labour and hon. members of the government ought to listen with some care to what I say tonight. The official position of the government is that it is in favour of paying government employees on the basis of comparability with the private sector. This is a principle with which my party agrees. As the critic on labour matters, I am quite prepared to say that this is an appropriate approach to be taken by any government in Canada.
I should like to bring to the attention of the House a situation in which the government, and generally speaking the country, are absolutely refusing to recognize the question of comparability. I refer to the Canadian Union of Professional and Technical Employees, and specifically 1 refer to the civil aviation inspectors in that group. This is not a large number of people, approximately 400. But, these people are completely responsible for civil aviation safety regulations in the country, and the flying public is completely dependent upon the government's ability to maintain within this group those competent and able people. I am not approaching this subject in a partisan manner, but I do not think there is any member in the House who would deny its importance.
I should like to emphasize what Mr. Walter McLeish, the head of the government's air transportation, said a few weeks ago. He indicated that the civil aviation inspectors are the backbone of the organization, in that they are in conjunction with other related officials the guardians of aviation safety in this country.
This group of civil aviation inspectors has not had a contract since 1975. If one looks at the total average income of the three subgroups within the aircraft operations group which comprises these people, one will find that the total average annual income is $25,240. A survey of 32 small independent aviation companies in Canada, on any comparability basis, indicates that the average annual income is $35,000. These people upon whom we depend to inspect and pass, for safety purposes, the other pilots of the country, are being paid $10,000 less.
The Canadian Airline Pilots Association has given me figures which show that in the current year for Air Canada the average annual wage for a pilot is $44,000 compared to $25,000 for those people who inspect the airplanes. At Canadian Pacific, the other major airline, the average wage for a pilot is $42,000 per year in comparison to $25,000 for the people who inspect the airplanes. We have here a situation where for a number of years we have grossly underpaid a small group of

people essential to the safety of aviation in Canada. The government, especially through my good friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell), has indicated that it wants public sector wage levels to be comparable to wage levels in the private sector and other sectors. The Treasury Board does not seem to have heard the minister or the government because their recent offer included an increase of only 5.7 per cent, which amounts to $1,425 per year.
We are facing a shameful situation in which the Government of Canada is deliberately and without justification, based upon a stated policy of comparability, not even giving these people, who have not had a contract for three years, an offer comparable with wages in the private sector. I realize there is necessity for restraint and for not allowing matters to get out of line, but I also realize that as of January 1, 1979, there were 50 vacancies in this vital group, and that since the beginning of January another ten people have left, increasing the number of vacancies to 60.
To the degree that we cannot maintain these highly qualified people, the whole safety system of aviation inspection in this country is in danger. The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) has remarked on this matter in the House. We have had some answers from the government side, but they have not been adequate. If the Government of Canada believes that the public service should be paid the same as those in the private sector-a principle with which I fully agree-then the time has come-

subtopic: STATISTICS CANADA-ABOLITION OF JOB VACANCY SURVEY
STATISTICS CANADA-ABOLITION OF JOB VACANCY SURVEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question to the Prime Minister yesterday was based on the premise that the job vacancy survey which has been done away with was a very important statistic which should not have been done away with lightly. It was a legitimate measure of the job demand and job opportunity for the hundreds of thousands of unemployed Canadians in this once stable and prosperous country.
In 1974, for example, there was an average number of job vacancies on a daily basis of 102,000. In 1978, the average number of job vacancies on a daily basis was 44,000. This means that only half the number of vacancies existed last year on a daily basis as existed four years ago. This is the part of the government's record of non-achievement, like the devastating $1 billion per month deficit, about which they do not like to have data published.
In the best traditions that existed years ago, when they would shoot the messenger who brought bad news, it appears someone-probably the chief statistician on instructions from the PMO-decided to do away with the embarrassing statistic that showed there were less than 50,000 jobs for the nearly one million unemployed in this country.
People like the president of the Canadian Labour Congress protested and wrote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) asking for a change in policy in this regard. I wanted to know the response given to Mr. McDermott's letter of last November. Instead the Prime Minister, for some reason, gave me an answer which had nothing to do with the question I asked but which referred to the consumer price index.
The minister responsible, and I hesitate to use that word referring to ministers across the aisle-the minister in charge, if I could use that instead-said that Statistics Canada placed a high priority on its labour surveys. If that is so, why did it abolish this important statistical adjunct of labour surveys?
Adjournment Debate
One must also ask why Statistics Canada is doing such a stupid, time-consuming, complicated, expensive survey as the one which has drawn so much fire recently in this House, while not being able to carry on the very legitimate and necessary measurement of jobs for Canadians?
The history of Statistics Canada's problems related to this and other matters goes back some distance. It is not just focussed in the recent criticisms of the C.D. Howe Institute or editorials in The Globe and Mail. It goes back beyond that, as most hon. members realize. In an article which appeared in the Toronto Sun on November 8, 1976, Doug Fisher wrote:
A top heavy executive structure, too many high salaried, well educated, under used, rank and perquisite conscious officers, topped by a boss who has lost control because the structure is too complex for him, not least because he's a relative outsider.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is having problems with Statistics Canada. He was once in charge of it when he was minister of industry, trade and commerce. In that respect, when questioned by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and myself on November 8, 1976, he said he would seek answers from the chief statistician to the vexing problem of unacceptably inaccurate data emanating from Statistics Canada about our national economy. This is the same minister who turned down my request for an inquiry into Statistics Canada and refused the wager of my seat against his regarding conditions in Statistics Canada. All of this is a matter of record. We must consider that only two years later the same minister, now in Finance, and, to use a paradox, in charge again of our national economy, has the gall to criticize Statistics Canada for sins it committed while he was in charge. One can check the minister's press conference of last August when he panned the data produced when he was, to use a misnomer, in charge. Were it not for the harm being done to the economy by the data being put out by Statistics Canada, it would be poetic justice if this minister, who is now being hampered by the data from Statistics Canada, were to be victimized, particularly when he had a chance while in charge to to something about it, instead of acting as an apologist. Perhaps the most alarming problem in Statistics Canada in relation to this issue is the number of complaints arising in the department, the number of grievances being Filed by the Public Service Alliance and the way in which these grievances are being dealt with when they reach higher levels. It shows dissatisfaction by the employees, so much so that The Globe and Mail in its July 4, 1978 editorial labelled our national statistical agency as "Sadistics Canada."
Speaking of surveys let us not forget the debacle of the costly and time consuming census done in 1971. This cost millions of dollars in terms of taxpayers' money, wasted time and money lost by the private sector. It was mishandled by this agency and it was never used as the committee minutes will reveal. We are not reassured on this side of the House when we find that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), either through inadvertence or lack of knowledge, confused some-

February 1, 1979
Adjournment Debate
thing as well known as the Consumer Price Index with the controversial job vacancy survey.
The president of the CLC wrote to the Prime Minister concerning this last fall, and that was the subject of my question. We need a shake up in Statistics Canada. We need a minister in charge of this department who understands a little about the elementary work and its terminology. We need to remind the Prime Minister that he too has some responsibility. We probably need a new chief statistician in the person of a top administrator. There are lots of people around, believe it or not, who could fill that position. For instance, Mr. Sylvain Cloutier is a name that comes to mind. He is a man with a proven track record in this regard.
We cannot tolerate any longer our national statistical agency seething with incompetence in the production of data, despite the apologists on the other side. It is obvious from the comments made by reputable financial institutions that it is hampering this country's economy-

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: STATISTICS CANADA-ABOLITION OF JOB VACANCY SURVEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the public expenditure cutbacks announced by the government last August, Statistics Canada's budget for next fiscal year has been reduced. Consequently this statistics agency had to examine and evaluate carefully all its on-going programs to see what could be cut back or discontinued.
The basic principle used in this task was to protect all the major national economic statistics. Except for these, however, all surveys were reviewed and classified by order of importance, the objective being to discontinue some. The job vacancy survey was considered of a lesser priority than other series which Statistics Canada continues to produce.
The decision to cancel the job vacancy survey was taken after consideration of the interest shown by the users for the information collected. After inquiries sent to individuals in the private sector as well as in the government, it was realized that the information on available positions was not systematically used by economists, political authorities nor by those who are responsible for programs nor by any other group of users. To that finding was added the fact that even if it had a general indicative value, the survey did not answer the administrative aims which have finally been felt to be more important. In addition, it was costly and quite burdensome for respondents.
The survey was launched as a result of a study made by Statistics Canada in co-operation with the Department of Employment and Immigration to determine the unfulfilled manpower demand. While Employment and Immigration Canada uses those data on vacant positions to establish its quotas per profession, it is a secondary use in relation with the

prime aim and there are less costly and more practical ways to meet that special need.
The collection of data for that survey has been cancelled. The last publication for 1978 will appear in March 1979. The calendar has been approved by the Department of Employment and Immigration.
In the last few years, Mr. Speaker, Canada was probably the only western country to make a regular job vacancy survey on a large scale. The United States abandoned theirs in 1973.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with the question I asked in the House on December 20 of last year of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) about the outrageous increase in pilotage rates in the Atlantic provinces by the Atlantic pilotage authority. I also raised the question last June in the House of Commons when the Atlantic pilotage authority first proposed these renewed increases in Atlantic Canada. I also raised it when the minister appeared before the transport committee on June 15, 1978. I pointed out to the minister that this would be the fourth increase in pilotage rates in Atlantic Canada since 1972.
The minister said they were giving $600,000 to the authority to help with their budget for this year, but that this would stop with his infamous user-pay principle and they had to be able to break even by 1980.
Large increases in pilotage fees were instituted in 1977 after tremendous opposition. Before 12 months had passed, the Atlantic pilotage authority with their voracious maw and insatiable propensity for spending money and increasing their fees were again looking for another increase. This went before the Canadian Transport Commission which held hearings in September. They compounded all of the errors and the felonies involved here by approving increases in excess of what the Atlantic pilotage authority had asked.
The commission approved an increase for small vessels of 62 per cent, for medium vessels of 30 per cent and for larger vessels of 18 per cent. This was at a time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was saying that we must practice restraint in Canada and keep down our wages and prices.
The Minister of Transport should get his black belt for destroying economic opportunities in the Atlantic provinces with this kind of policy, permitting what he agrees is an unsatisfactory situation. The minister says he is not satisfied with the pilotage set-up in Canada and that he will bring in legislation. Why does he not act to stop this huge increase in costs for shipping in the Atlantic provinces?
If the Minister of Transport is left to have his way, he will make a desert of the port of St. John's and other ports in Atlantic Canada. He is choking port business by allowing these huge increases in fees.
February 1, 1979

Today the Board of Economic Development Ministers announced shipbuilding assistance. What they announced was very stingy, but it will be assistance. They are going to carry out a program. They talked about assistance to the drydock in St. John's and other drydocks. What is the good of that if foreign vessels will not come into our ports because of the huge increase in pilotage fees?
The increases were approved and went into effect on January 22. We only learned of them a week later. They were in effect before we knew about them. I want to quote Captain Douglas Latter, chairman of the authority, as follows:
Latter said a drop in expected revenues from the recent fee increase may force these fees even higher next year.
The authority has calculated the higher fees will derive a 21 per cent increase in revenues, if shipping remains at 1978 levels.
But traffic in the harbours of Atlantic Canada is down 12 per cent from the previous year and it may go down even more despite these increases. In fact, it will probably go down because of the increases in pilotage fees. Then they will come back and ask for another increase next year.
This is a policy of choking the ports of Atlantic Canada. There must be a thorough investigation of this situation. The minister should ask that these increases not go into effect. Why the discrimination against small vessels? How can we attract foreign fleets into our ports if we impose these increases of 69 per cent? Take, for example, Spanish pair trawlers previously paid $650 for pilotage inward and outward at the city of St. John's and movement within the port. That fee will increase to $1,100 under the new system, a 69 per cent increase. For a single Spanish trawler the increase will be 48 per cent, from $370 to $550. We spent three years persuading the Spanish fishing fleet to come back to the city of St. John's to conduct their business instead of St. Pierre and Miquelon, the French territories, and now we are going to lose it again because of these huge increases.
Not only that, but the increases originally advertized by the Atlantic pilotage authority are not the increases which have gone into effect. The Canadian Transport Commission which is supposed to defend the consumer approved increases larger than were asked for by the Atlantic pilotage authority. Take the port of St. John's, for example. I will put on record the number of vessels using that port last year. There were 780 vessels of 1,828,000 tons which were Canadian-owned. This shows the small size of the vessels. In addition, there were 846 foreign vessels with a gross tonnage of 1,591,000. Again, this shows how small the vessels are. The increase to which I have referred will hurt the city of St. John's more than any other port in the Atlantic provinces. Of those foreign vessels, 180
Adjournment Debate
were Portuguese trawlers, 100 were Russian trawlers, some 215 were Spanish trawlers. These increases of between 50 and 60 per cent are going to strike that traffic. How can we become the service centre of the North Atlantic in St. John's, in Halifax, in Saint John, New Brunswick, and the rest of the Atlantic ports if the government is going to permit these huge cost increases to be levied on users without concern to the efficiency with which the operation is run?
This is a quasi-independent operation. Why, for instance, should pilots in St. John's be paid on the same basis as pilots in Halifax? Pilots in Halifax have to go out ten miles to bring a ship in while in St. John's they might have to go out a mile, perhaps. In St. John's today we have several class A pilots who were originally supposed to bring tankers in and out of the Come-By-Chance oil refinery; they are now bringing in small vessels yet they have to be paid at the rates applicable to class A pilots. Surely this is not necessary. All kinds of changes could be made to reduce these costs but the government does not care. Apparently the government is not fazed by these huge increases. What is the good of giving assistance to the dockyard at St. John's, putting in a synchro-lift, if we are scaring off potential traffic? Here is Atlantic Canada on the verge of a breakthrough at last in these areas-

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Under the Pilotage Act, Mr. Speaker, pilotage authorities should establish fair and reasonable rates which would enable them to make some profits and to accrue all other income needed to finance their own operations.
When the act came into force in 1972, we were aware that considerable increases would be necessary to attain that objective but we hoped that the four pilotage authorities would become financially autonomous from three to five years later. The Pacific and Laurentian pilotage authorities have already achieved that end and consequently they do not need any government subsidy. The Great Lakes and Atlantic pilotage authorities recently published new rates which, according to them, will enable them to become financially autonomous within two years. As foreseen in the act, representations were made to the Canadian Transport Commission which held public hearings and made a decision in each case. As far as the Atlantic region is concerned, the commission recommends an increase in the rates established by the port of St. John's, an increase of 40 per cent for small vessels, 25 per cent for average vessels and 35 per cent for larger vessels.
